cues.text: From Innkeeper to Empress's Household

Born around the middle of the third century, probably at Drepanum on the Nicomedian Gulf in Bithynia, Helena came from plainly humble origins — St. Ambrose, preaching decades after her death, described her frankly as a stabularia, an inn-keeper.
Whatever her exact social station, she became united to the rising Roman military officer Constantius Chlorus.
In 274, at Naissus in Upper Moesia, she bore him her only child, a son named Constantine, who would remain devoted to her for the rest of her long life.
Set Aside for a Throne

When Constantius was raised to the rank of Caesar in 293 under Diocletian's new imperial system, dynastic necessity required a marriage into the reigning house, and he set Helena aside to wed Theodora, stepdaughter of the senior emperor Maximian.

A later medieval legend claiming Helena was herself the daughter of a British king has no historical foundation and appears to rest on a misreading of an ancient panegyric rather than any genuine record.

Whatever grief this separation cost her, it never touched her son's own loyalty; Constantine kept faith with his mother even as the political world around them reordered itself without regard for either of them.
Augusta
Constantius died in 306, and the army at once proclaimed Constantine his successor.
Among the new emperor's first acts was summoning Helena to the imperial court and conferring on her the exalted title Augusta.
He ordered that she be honored throughout the empire as mother of the sovereign; coins were struck bearing her likeness.
It was under her son's influence, following his decisive victory over Maxentius in 312, that Helena embraced the Christian faith.
The historian Eusebius, who knew her personally, testifies that she became so devout a servant of God.
One might have believed her a disciple of the Redeemer from her very childhood—a late conversion, but a complete one.
We recognize in it a grace that comes, for some souls, only after long years of waiting.
A Pilgrimage to the Holy Land
In her old age, around 326 to 328, Helena undertook an extended journey through Palestine and the eastern provinces.
She distributed alms generously along the way and, according to Eusebius's own eyewitness account, oversaw construction of great basilicas at Bethlehem and on the Mount of Olives.
The Bethlehem basilica stood on the site venerated as Christ's birth, while the Mount of Olives basilica marked the place of his Ascension.

A venerable tradition, first recorded within a generation of her death by St. Ambrose and elaborated by later historians such as Rufinus, holds that during this same journey she also recovered relics of the True Cross at Jerusalem.

The Church has cherished this tradition for sixteen centuries, even as the exact circumstances of the discovery rest on devotional memory passed down by the faithful rather than on a contemporary eyewitness record.
A Simplicity Amid Splendor
Though she now commanded the resources of the imperial treasury, Eusebius records that Helena moved among ordinary worshippers with striking humility.
She dressed modestly, kneeling among the common faithful rather than apart from them, and used her position to secure the release of prisoners and exiles.
She also relieved the poor wherever her intercession could reach.
It is a detail worth holding onto: a woman raised in a single lifetime from an inn-keeper's obscurity to the very summit of Roman power, who let that ascent enlarge her charity rather than her pride.
Legacy
Helena died around the year 330, with her son at her side, at what Eusebius reckons was roughly eighty years of age.
Constantine had already renamed her native Drepanum in her honor as Helenopolis, and her body was afterward brought to Constantinople.

Venerated ever since as one of the great women of the Constantinian age and honored today as patroness of converts, archaeologists, and those who have known difficult or broken marriages, Helena remains a witness.
For every believer who has ever felt set aside or overlooked, her quiet, late-flowering fidelity can still leave behind a legacy.
It is a legacy of pilgrimage, building, and searching out what the world had buried, outlasting the very throne from which she once seemed excluded.
